column1: Indicator 5: Top-level policies and measures for monitoring and reaching out to non-enrolled youth, 2024/2025 - Policy description and references/links
column2: Unnamed: 1
Policy description
There is collaboration with municipalities, especially in Brussels, involving local prevention units and partnerships with the non-profit organisation Foyer, which serves Roma and Travelers.

Since 2018, a data linkage has been in place between Education and the VDAB database to better map these young people. As a result, the Flemish government can identify early school leavers who are neither pursuing education, training, or other forms of education, nor employed.

Schooling is mandatory until age 16, but students have the right to continue their education afterward. Free transportation is offered to all students who travel to schools outside their residential area, including those over 16 who choose to continue their studies. Additionally, free textbooks are available for students from 1st to 12th grade. Students over 16 who continue studying can receive social benefits until age 20. Youth mentorship programmes and access to youth and community centers are also available for students over 16 who remain in education through 12th grade.

The framework for addressing non-enrolled youth ensures social inclusion and educational continuity for individuals up to 18 years. It involves collaboration with local authorities and non-profits, addressing absenteeism issues. Students receive free transportation, textbooks, and social benefits to support education beyond compulsory schooling. Guided by the Social and Legal Protection of Children Act, it includes youth mentorship, community centre involvement, and home visits. Municipal authorities conduct field social work and outreach with at-risk families. Awareness campaigns funded by the Ministry of Education highlight the importance of education and preventing risky behaviour. Trained social workers monitor progress to align measures with individual needs, following guidelines like the Methodological Recommendation on Social Work with Families at Risk.

The Kommunale Ungeindsats (KUI) is a municipal initiative dedicated to supporting individuals under 25 who have completed primary education but have not yet pursued secondary education or secured full-time employment (at least 20 hours per week). KUI's primary objective is to guide these young people towards further education or work opportunities. To achieve this, KUI collaborates with the individual to develop an education plan that coordinates resources and initiatives from the education, employment, and social units within the municipality, aiming to facilitate their transition into secondary education or employment.

Community-based youth outreach includes several initiatives to aid young people's transition from school to work. Outreach youth social work targets those avoiding traditional services, offering professional guidance in public spaces. The JOBLINGE programme collaborates with businesses and government to combat youth unemployment through mentorship and vocational training. The Federal Employment Agency supports career orientation with online and personal counselling. Comprehensive support involves early preventative services, awareness campaigns with information about training programmes and jobs, customised funding, and a training guarantee that includes internships and mobility grants. Youth employment agencies promote cooperation among agencies for streamlined support. Additionally, the ESF Plus Programme "JUGEND STÄRKEN: Brücken in die Eigenständigkeit" supports young adults aged 14 to 26 with socio-educational resources to manage independent living aspects like housing and education.

The National Programme of Support Measures for NEETs (2023–2029) facilitates mobile youth work and youth centres to aid NEETs with basic or lower education in continuing their studies. The Youth Guarantee Support System targets individuals aged 16–29, assisting in their re-entry into education or the labour market. The proportion of NEETs is consistently monitored through the Estonian Education Information System, as well as the data from the Social Insurance Board, the Unemployment Insurance Fund, and the Employment Register.

The regulatory framework for protecting minors in Spain, established by the Organic Law 1/1996 and Law 26/2015, supports various regional initiatives aimed at education and social integration. Community-based outreach programmes, supported by grants from the Ministry of Education, help combat educational inequalities, monitor school absenteeism, and provide socio-educational activities. Home visits and counselling are part of regional plans to address absenteeism, as seen in Aragón. Financial and material assistance, including scholarships like Andalucía's Beca 6000 and Second Chance Scholarship, support students over 16 to prevent dropout and encourage continued education. Youth mentorship programmes, such as those in Castilla-La Mancha and Valencia, pair mentors with students to enhance academic and personal development, while youth and community centres offer diverse activities for ages 14-30. Awareness campaigns, as defined in the País Vasco, aim to inform and engage society in supporting education and youth development, forming a comprehensive approach to addressing the needs of young people.

Community-based outreach for adolescents and young adults includes programmes like FOQUALE (i.e. Training-Qualification-Employment Networks), which coordinate school and partner efforts to provide personalised paths back to education or work. The Mission de lutte contre le décrochage scolaire (MLDS) and "Return to School Structures" support the reintegration of school dropouts, while the Campus des métiers et des qualifications (CMQ) enhances vocational training opportunities. "Missions locales" facilitate home visits and counselling to address dropouts' needs and ease re-enrollment. Financial assistance, such as mobility aid and the youth commitment contract (CEJ), helps overcome economic barriers to education. Youth mentorship programmes under "1 jeune / 1 solution" offer individualised support, with the "1 jeune - 1 mentor" plan launched in 2021 to boost youth autonomy. Awareness campaigns within this framework highlight training opportunities for school dropouts. Regular monitoring and reporting, through the interministerial information exchange system (SIEI) and drop-out follow-up and support platforms (PSAD), ensure comprehensive identification and intervention for youth dropping out of school.

The National Youth Programme for 2023 to 2025 aims to enhance local and regional youth policies by providing financial grants to develop respective youth programmes. These projects will actively involve young people, especially those with fewer opportunities, in designing relevant measures and activities. The activities will also engage out-of-school youth.

The orientation reform, Mission 4-C1, introduces orientation modules in secondary schools and a digital platform to link education, universities, and the labour market, helping students make informed choices and reducing dropout and NEET rates. These modules personalise and broaden study plans, integrating hands-on learning and extracurricular activities to explore students' skills and interests. Guidelines from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR) aim to connect education cycles, support thoughtful choices, and reduce dropouts, enabling access to tertiary education. Collaborations with local communities, educational institutions, and the labour market support this networked process. Secondary schools offer 30-hour orientation modules yearly, documented in E-Portfolios and supported by digital platforms for teachers and families. The PNRR funds 15-hour orientation courses in upper secondary schools through university partnerships. Supported by the UNICA platform and national assessment by INVALSI, these initiatives align with the NEET Plan's phased approach to tackle youth inactivity, involving the Youth Guarantee, Youth Desks at Employment Centres, and the Universal Civil Service.

Second chance evening schools are offered for citizens aged 19 and above, free of tuition or expenses. The Ministry of Labor maintains records of youth over 19 who have not completed upper secondary education. To support these individuals, the educational counseling services at the Ministry of Education work collaboratively with the Ministry of Labor to encourage enrollment in evening schools. This collaboration is legally supported; the Council of Ministers established the National Body for Lifelong Guidance in 2009, chaired by the Ministers of Education, Sports and Youth, and Labor and Social Insurance, to address the educational needs of these young citizens.

The Youth International Programmes Agency leverages EU and municipal support to offer young people numerous project opportunities. It provides guidance on drafting projects, shares valuable information about European opportunities, and fosters experience exchanges. The Agency manages several EU programmes, such as "Erasmus+" for youth, the "European Solidarity Corps," and oversees the European Commission's youth information network "Eurodesk." It also supports "eTwinning," the national Youth Policy Programme, and projects like "Development of the Digital Youth Work System in Local Governments" and "NAMELY and DO 2.0." Continuing from previous EU funding periods, the "NAMELY and DO 2.0 for NEET Youth" project aims to enhance skills for individuals aged 15-29 who are not in education, employment, or training (NEET), encouraging their participation in educational and vocational activities, employment opportunities, or involvement with NGOs and youth centres.

The community-based outreach includes the Multidimensional Family Therapy Programme, targeting behavioral issues in 11-17-year-olds to help reintegrate them into education and social norms. Home visits and counseling through case management provide comprehensive support to prevent rights violations. Preventive services, such as social skills development and family conferences, aim to strengthen family dynamics. "Jungtys," a mentorship programme for 14-29-year-olds from 2024-2028, focuses on reducing youth inactivity by facilitating reentry into the labour market or education through personalised plans. Financial and material assistance ensures school transportation and covers costs for supplies and meals under the Law on Education and under the Law on Social Support for Students. Youth and community centers offer day social care to develop life skills. The Student Register and NEMIS system track uneducated children and dropouts to address their return to education.

The National Youth Service (SNJ) proactively monitors and engages school dropouts to encourage their reintegration into education or the workforce. By leveraging monthly dropout lists, agents reach out to young individuals for initial interviews, employing diverse communication methods if initial contact is unresponsive. SNJ offers tailored support and a variety of flexible, practical programmes, such as voluntary services, workshops, internships, orientation classes, and training, to help young people aged 16 to 30 gain experience and skills. The workshops, spread across three sites, attract a diverse group, including international protection beneficiaries, and focus on creative skills, such as woodworking and sewing. The SNJ also coordinates annual events like the "Deng Zukunft, Däi Wee" fair and the Engagement Evening, which connect youth with career opportunities and recognise their efforts in transition projects. A Dropout Report, developed in collaboration with the Ministry of National Education, provides systematic data analysis to effectively monitor and address dropout rates.

Community-based outreach and youth and community centres are facilitated by Agenzija Zghazagh, a government agency focused on youth outreach and inclusion. While their services extend beyond just supporting unenrolled youth, they play a crucial role in youth development. Youth Cafes provide safe, alternative leisure spaces for individuals aged 13 to 25 to interact with peers, explore talents, and enhance personal and social skills. Youth Hubs offer a recreational setting where youth workers collaborate with young people on projects and initiatives to unlock their potential. Detached Youth Work involves youth workers engaging with young people in discussions and informing them about various opportunities and issues.

Together with schools and municipalities, the government is implementing measures to encourage students to return to education. As a result of the decentralized system,  top-level authorities primarily provide the financial backing, while the execution of most actions is carried out by schools and municipalities.

The Compulsory Training Act (Ausbildungspflichtgesetz), introduced in 2016, mandates that all young people under 18 who have completed compulsory schooling and are permanently resident in Austria must continue with education or training. This obligation remains in effect until they reach 18 or successfully complete additional education or training. To ensure compliance, young people under 18 are monitored for enrollment in education or apprenticeship programmes. Youth Coaching is a supportive counselling programme designed for those finishing mandatory schooling or who have dropped out, offering personalised assistance to help them re-enter the educational system or secure an apprenticeship. Youth coaches also provide counselling for those who are not in education, employment, or training (NEET).

The Youth Employment Initiative (YEI), part of Poland’s Knowledge Education Development Programme, was funded by the European Social Fund (ESF), the Youth Employment Initiative (YEI) budget, and the state budget, with over EUR 5.4 billion allocated, including more than EUR 2 billion specifically for youth support. It aims to activate unemployed young people under 30 through vocational guidance, training, internships, apprenticeships, subsidised employment, business grants, and mobility support. Targeting regions with youth unemployment above 25%, support was extended nationwide to include those aged 15-29, particularly NEETs (Not in Employment, Education, or Training), benefiting around 700,000 young people. Additionally, the 2023-2024 “Time for the Young” pilot programme, backed by PLN 60 million from the Labour Fund, established 76 advisory centres offering vocational, psychological, educational, financial, and housing support. Implemented by the Ministry of Labour, Family and Social Policy, the initiative involved collaboration between labour offices, training institutions, NGOs, and social services to enhance youth employment and social inclusion.

The annual national report on education, chapters 1 and 5 cover the essential statistical indicators for national monitoring and reporting the rate of enrolled vs. not enrolled students for all levels of education.  This form of monitoring and reporting is constant and consistent from year to year and it supports the initiatives for reaching out the non-enrolled youth through targeted initiatives like research-based surveys, studies and support inititiatives.

PUM-o+ is a dynamic, project-based programme designed for young adults (ages 15-26) who have dropped out or failed to complete basic, lower, or upper secondary education. It also supports students at risk of dropping out and younger participants in the Adult Basic School programme. This initiative empowers vulnerable young people by helping them re-enter education or the job market, discover their talents, develop essential skills, and break free from the cycle of failure. The programme is implemented by the Ministry of Labour, Family, Social Affairs and Equal Opportunities, in collaboration with the Employment Service of the Republic of Slovenia and other external partners. It is co-financed by the European Social Fund as part of the European Cohesion Policy Programme 2021-2027.

Outreach youth work provides safe and confidential support for young people under 29, helping them access essential services, education, and employment opportunities. It is voluntary and focuses on empowerment, independence, and social participation. The Regional State Administrative Agency allocates over €50 million annually for youth-related initiatives, including One-Stop Guidance Centers, which offer free assistance on various life matters for those under 30. Workshop activities foster inclusion, skill development, and career readiness through multidisciplinary collaboration. Additionally, Save the Children Finland’s mentoring programme supports middle school students in their studies, fostering motivation, confidence, and learning success. The National Audit Office (VTV) has made efforts to identify, support, and reintegrate young people disengaged from work and education. Its January 2025 report reveals that 9% of 15–29-year-olds have been neither working nor studying in recent years, and in 2023, one in five 20–24-year-olds had only completed comprehensive school.

Municipalities are responsible for identifying relevant local and civil society actors—such as schools, social services, and employment agencies—for collaboration in supporting young people. This cooperation should be outlined in an action plan with measurable goals and expected outcomes. Through  the municipal activity responsibility (KAA), municipalities must monitor and offer tailored support to individuals under 20 who are not in upper secondary education. These efforts, aimed at motivating youth to start or resume education, must be continuous, documented, and tracked in a municipal register.

As part of the government's action plan to reduce youth violence, a study and career counselor has been appointed to support and engage children who are not in education, employment, or training (NEET). Youth and community centers remain open to all children, with a particular focus on vulnerable groups. Additionally, the government has partially funded a traveling youth center aimed at reaching 12–16-year-olds who do not participate in extracurricular activities, exhibit negative communication patterns, engage in risky behavior, or face social challenges.

The Law on Vocational Education allows students who have started but not completed their education to continue as part-time students. These students attend preparatory (instructional-consultative) classes and take exams to progress in their studies. Schools provide guidance on education pathways and organize structured support to help students develop essential skills and successfully complete their education.

The county authority is required to provide follow-up services for young people who are entitled to education and training under Section 5-1 of the Education Act (upper secondary education) and who are neither enrolled in education nor employed, as outlined in Section 9-4 of the Education Act. These services must be available until the end of the year in which the individual turns 24.

Targeted measures for Roma students, who are the majority of non-enrolled youth, focus on increasing primary school enrollment to 90% and secondary school completion to 50% by 2030. These efforts include community outreach in collaboration with local authorities and ministries, as well as enforcing regulations to prevent the wrongful placement of Roma students in special education. Progress includes a rise in secondary school enrollment from 22% in 2014 to 28% in 2019, with an 85.4% primary school enrollment rate and a 7% reduction in dropout rates.

National policy outlines provisions for young people above the compulsory school age who require guidance to complete their education. It emphasises providing personalised support to help these individuals finish their schooling, with the aim of ensuring they have the necessary resources, advice, and opportunities. The guidance process includes regular monitoring and tailored educational pathways to encourage completion and facilitate further career or academic goals.
